The T-SQL statement that defines a new table and its columns is {{c1::CREATE TABLE}}.
column2:
Specify the data type and relevant column rules in the definition.
Review source

column1: In an uncompressed SQL Server row, an INT value uses {{c1::4 bytes}}.
column2:
Choose the integer width according to the required range.
Review source

column1: In an uncompressed SQL Server row, a BIGINT value uses {{c1::8 bytes}}.
column2:
BIGINT provides a larger range than INT at a greater storage width.
Review source

column1: In DECIMAL(p,s), p specifies the {{c1::total number of digits}}.
column2:
Precision counts digits on both sides of the decimal point.
Review source

column1: In DECIMAL(p,s), s specifies the {{c1::number of digits after the decimal point}}.
column2:
Scale is part of the total precision, not an additional allowance.
Review source

column1: An uncompressed DECIMAL(10,2) value requires {{c1::9 bytes}}.
column2:
Precision 10 falls in the 10-to-19-digit storage band, not the five-byte band.
Review source

column1: In VARCHAR(n), n limits the string's {{c1::byte length}}.
column2:
With multibyte encodings, this is not a guarantee of n characters.
Review source

column1: SQL Server DATETIME2 supports up to {{c1::7}} fractional-second digits.
column2:
This describes precision, not a guarantee of clock accuracy.
Review source

column1: SQL Server's document-oriented data type for XML content is {{c1::XML}}.
column2:
It stores XML documents rather than treating the content as an ordinary string column.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server 2025, the native JSON data type stores documents in a {{c1::binary format}}.
column2:
The format is designed for efficient storage, reads, and updates.
Review source

column1: A SQL Server UNIQUEIDENTIFIER value uses {{c1::16 bytes}}.
column2:
It stores a globally unique identifier, commonly called a GUID.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server, IDENTITY(100,5) has an initial seed of {{c1::100}}.
column2:
The first argument specifies the starting identity value.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server, IDENTITY(100,5) has an increment of {{c1::5}}.
column2:
The second argument specifies the identity step.
Review source

column1: A SQL Server identity column still needs a PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE rule to enforce {{c1::uniqueness}}.
column2:
The IDENTITY property alone does not enforce uniqueness.
Review source

column1: A DATETIME2 column can use DEFAULT ({{c1::SYSUTCDATETIME()}}) for a current UTC insertion timestamp.
column2:
UTC means Coordinated Universal Time, and this function returns DATETIME2 with higher fractional precision than GETUTCDATE.
Review source

column1: In analytical modeling, a {{c1::fact table}} stores measurable events.
column2:
Examples include sales transactions and their measures.
Review source

column1: In analytical modeling, a {{c1::dimension table}} provides descriptive context for measured events.
column2:
Examples include product or customer attributes.
Review source

column1: Given Quantity INT NOT NULL DEFAULT (0), an INSERT that omits Quantity receives {{c1::0}}.
column2:
This assumes an ordinary successful INSERT with no trigger changing the value.
Review source
